title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 837–839 (Night 186, continuing nights-185), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 186 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Maymūna crows over Dahnash that her beloved has shown himself proud and aloof while Budūr went mad with love for him, and declares that she forgives him; she writes him a deed, and bids Qashqash help Dahnash carry Budūr home before the night runs out. The two ifrits fly the princess back to her own bed, and Maymūna stays alone gazing at the sleeping Qamar al-Zamān until the night is nearly gone. At dawn Qamar al-Zamān wakes to find the girl gone. Guessing that his father has spirited her away to sharpen his wish to marry, he says his dawn prayer and then demands the truth from the servant Ṣawāb, who swears that no one, male or female, came through the locked door. Sure that his father has taught the servant to lie, Qamar al-Zamān throws him to the ground, kicks and throttles him until he faints, then ties him to the well rope and dunks him again and again in the winter-cold water, swearing not to pull him out until he tells him who took the girl. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-sixth night,
sentences.n: al-sādisa, “the sixth”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ لَمَّا نَامَتْ بِجَانِبِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَجَرَى مِنْهَا مَا جَرَى قَالَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ لِدَهْنَشَ هَلْ رَأَيْتَ يَا مَلْعُونُ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ مَعْشُوقِي مِنَ التِّيهِ وَالدَّلَالِ وَكَيْفَ فَعَلَتْ مَعْشُوقَتُكَ مِنَ الْوَلَهِ بِمَعْشُوقِي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malikata Budūra lammā nāmat bi-jānibi Qamari al-Zamāni wa-jarā minhā mā jarā qālat Maymūnatu li-Dahnasha hal raʾayta yā malʿūnu kayfa faʿala maʿshūqī mina al-tīhi wa-al-dalāli wa-kayfa faʿalat maʿshūqatuka mina al-walahi bi-maʿshūqī
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-Queen Budūr, when she-slept at-the-side (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-there-passed from-her what passed, said Maymūna to-Dahnash: Did you-see, O accursed-one, how acted my-beloved from the-haughtiness and-the-coyness, and-how acted your-beloved (f.) from the-love-madness for-my-beloved?
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Queen Budūr had fallen asleep beside Qamar al-Zamān, after all that she had done, Maymūna said to Dahnash, “Did you see, you accursed one, how my beloved bore himself, all pride and disdain, and how your beloved behaved, mad with love for mine?
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story by recalling where the last night ended, with Budūr asleep at Qamar al-Zamān's side. As before, the print runs السعيد and ان together as one word, السعيدان; the spacing is kept, and the pair is read al-saʿīdu anna. The sentence begun with anna is never finished: after the lammā clause a new main clause starts, qālat Maymūnatu, “Maymūna said”, a loose join common in this narration. jarā minhā mā jarā, “there passed from her what passed”, a discreet formula for what the reader has just seen. malʿūn, “accursed”, passive participle of laʿana, “to curse”, is her sharp way of addressing Dahnash. faʿala min, “to act out of”: min gives the source of the behaviour. tīh, “haughtiness”, and dalāl, “coquetry, the airs of a beloved”: Maymūna makes Qamar al-Zamān's unbroken sleep into a beloved's proud indifference. walah, “distraction, love-madness”; bi- marks its object, “for my beloved”. maʿshūq, “beloved”, is the passive participle of ʿashiqa, “to love passionately”, feminine maʿshūqa. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَا شَكَّ أَنَّ مَعْشُوقِي أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مَعْشُوقَتِكَ وَلٰكِنِّي عَفَوْتُ عَنْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lā shakka anna maʿshūqī aḥsanu min maʿshūqatika wa-lākinnī ʿafawtu ʿanka
sentences.l: And-no doubt that my-beloved (is) more-beautiful than your-beloved (f.); but-I have-pardoned (from) you.
sentences.i: There is no doubt that my beloved is lovelier than yours; but I forgive you.”
sentences.n: lā shakka, “there is no doubt”: lā of absolute negation, with its noun in the accusative and without tanwīn. aḥsanu min, “better, more beautiful than”, the elative with min. By the test Qashqash proposed, whichever of the pair burned more for the other was the lesser, and Budūr has gone further than Qamar al-Zamān, so Maymūna claims the victory. ʿafā ʿan, “to pardon, let off”: ʿan marks the one let off, here Dahnash for his boast.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَتْ لَهُ وَثِيقَةً أَنَّهُ أَعْتَقَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma katabat lahu wathīqatan annahu aʿtaqahā
sentences.l: Then she-wrote for-him a-deed that-he had-freed-her.
sentences.i: Then she wrote out a deed for him, that he had set her free.
sentences.n: wathīqa, “a deed, written warrant”; li- marks the one it is written for. aʿtaqa, Form IV, “to set (a slave) free”, the word of manumission. The pronouns are puzzling as printed: annahu aʿtaqahā says “that he freed her”, though it is Maymūna who has just pardoned Dahnash, and the expected sense is a deed of release for him, “that she had freed him”, which would be annahā aʿtaqathu. Perhaps the clause has been garbled; perhaps the deed is meant to state that Dahnash released her from the dispute. The letters are kept and read as they stand; the sense is uncertain.

sentences.t: وَالْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى قَشْقَشَ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ ادْخُلْ مَعَ دَهْنَشَ وَاحْمِلْ مَعْشُوقَتَهُ وَسَاعِدْهُ عَلَى وُصُولِهَا إِلَى مَكَانِهَا لِأَنَّ اللَّيْلَ قَدْمَضَى وَلَمْ يَبْقَ مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: wa-iltafatat ilā Qashqasha wa-qālat lahu udkhul maʿa Dahnasha wa-iḥmil maʿshūqatahu wa-sāʿidhu ʿalā wuṣūlihā ilā makānihā li-anna al-layla qad maḍā wa-lam yabqa minhu illā qalīlan
sentences.l: And-she-turned to Qashqash and-said to-him: Go-in with Dahnash and-carry his-beloved (f.), and-help-him in her-arriving at her-place; because the-night has passed and-not remained of-it except a-little.
sentences.i: And she turned to Qashqash and said to him, “Go in with Dahnash, carry his beloved, and help him get her back to her place, for the night is spent and little of it is left.”
sentences.n: iltafata ilā, Form VIII, “to turn to”. udkhul maʿa, “go in with”, that is, set to work alongside him. sāʿada ʿalā, Form III, “to help with”: ʿalā marks the task, here wuṣūlihā, “her arriving”, a verbal noun. li-anna, “because”: li-, “for”, with anna, “that”. The print runs قد and مضى together as one word, قدمضى; the spacing is kept. illā qalīlan, “except a little”: after a negative verb whose subject is the excepted word, Classical Arabic puts it in the nominative, illā qalīlun; the accusative here is a habit of later Arabic, which tends to put any word after illā in the accusative. It is read as printed. A line later the narrator writes illā al-qalīlu, in the nominative.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And-he-said: (With) hearing and-obedience.
sentences.i: And he answered with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”, the stock formula of assent, in the accusative as if governed by an unspoken verb: “(I give) hearing and obedience”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ قَشْقَشُ وَدَهْنَشُ إِلَى الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ وَدَخَلَا تَحْتَهَا وَحَمَلَاهَا وَطَارَابِهَا وَأَوْصَلَاهَا إِلَى مَكَانِهَا وَأَرْقَدَاهَا فِي فِرَاشِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama Qashqashu wa-Dahnashu ilā al-malikati Budūra wa-dakhalā taḥtahā wa-ḥamalāhā wa-ṭārā bihā wa-awṣalāhā ilā makānihā wa-arqadāhā fī firāshihā
sentences.l: Then came-forward Qashqash and-Dahnash to the-Queen Budūr, and-the-two-went under-her and-the-two-carried-her and-the-two-flew with-her and-the-two-brought-her to her-place and-the-two-laid-her-down in her-bed.
sentences.i: Then Qashqash and Dahnash came up to Queen Budūr, got underneath her and lifted her, flew off with her, brought her back to her own place and laid her down in her bed.
sentences.n: taqaddama, “came forward”, stands in the singular before its two subjects, as Classical Arabic has a verb do when it comes first; once the pair has been named, the verbs that follow take the dual ending -ā: dakhalā, ḥamalāhā, ṭārā, awṣalāhā, arqadāhā. The print runs طارا and بها together as one word, وطارابها; the spacing is kept, and it is read wa-ṭārā bihā, “and the two flew with her”: ṭāra bi-, “to fly off with”, with bi- of accompaniment. awṣala, Form IV, “to bring (someone) to”, and arqada, Form IV, “to lay down to sleep”.

sentences.t: وَاخْتَلَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ بِالنَّظَرِ إِلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَهُوَ نَائِمٌ حَتَّى لَمْ يَبْقَ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ إِلَّا الْقَلِيلُ ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهَتْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ikhtalat Maymūnatu bi-al-naẓari ilā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-huwa nāʾimun ḥattā lam yabqa mina al-layli illā al-qalīlu thumma tawajjahat ilā ḥāli sabīlihā
sentences.l: And-was-alone Maymūna with-the-gazing at Qamar al-Zamān while-he (was) sleeping, until not remained of the-night except the-little; then she-headed to (the) state (of) her-way.
sentences.i: And Maymūna stayed alone, gazing at Qamar al-Zamān as he slept, until only a little of the night was left; then she went on her way.
sentences.n: ikhtalā bi-, Form VIII, “to be alone with, withdraw with”: bi- marks what one keeps private company with, here the gazing itself; Maymūna has the sleeper to herself. wa-huwa nāʾimun, “and he sleeping”, a circumstantial clause with wa-. The ئ of نائم is printed. illā al-qalīlu stands in the nominative, as Classical Arabic has it, beside illā qalīlan just before. tawajjaha ilā ḥāli sabīlihā, “she headed off on her way”: ḥāl sabīlihā, “the state of her road”, is a set phrase of later Arabic for going about one's business.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْشَقَّ الْفَجْرُ انْتَبَهَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ فَالْتَفَتَ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَلَمْ يَجِدِ الصَّبِيَّةَ عِنْدَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā inshaqqa al-fajru intabaha Qamaru al-Zamāni min manāmihi fa-iltafata yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-lam yajidi al-ṣabiyyata ʿindahu
sentences.l: And-when split-open the-dawn, woke Qamar al-Zamān from his-sleep, and-turned right and-left, and-not he-found the-girl with-him.
sentences.i: When dawn broke, Qamar al-Zamān woke from his sleep and looked to his right and his left, but did not find the girl beside him.
sentences.n: inshaqqa, Form VII, “to split open”: the dawn “splits” the dark. intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake”. yamīnan wa-shimālan, “right and left”, adverbial accusatives. lam yajidi, jussive of wajada, “to find”, takes a helping kasra before the article.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَاهٰذَا الْأَمْرُ كَأَنَّ أَبِي يُرَغِّبُنِي فِى الزَّوَاجِ بِالصَّبِيَّةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ عِنْدِي ثُمَّ أَخَذَهَا سِرّاً لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تَزْدَادَ رَغْبَتِي فِي الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fī nafsihi mā hādhā al-amru ka-anna abī yuraghghibunī fī al-zawāji bi-al-ṣabiyyati allatī kānat ʿindī thumma akhadhahā sirran li-ajli an tazdāda raghbatī fī al-zawāji
sentences.l: And-he-said in himself: What (is) this the-matter? As-if my-father (is) making-me-desirous of the-marriage with-the-girl who was with-me, then took-her secretly, for-the-sake that should-increase my-desire for the-marriage.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “What is this? It must be that my father is trying to make me want to marry the girl who was with me, and has taken her away in secret so that my desire to marry may grow.”
sentences.n: The print runs ما and هذا together as one word, ماهذا; the spacing is kept. ka-anna, “as if”: ka-, “like”, with anna, “that”, here “it seems that”; its hamza and shadda are printed. raghghaba fī, Form II, “to make (someone) desire”: fī marks what is desired. al-zawāj bi-, “marriage to”: bi- marks the partner. Qamar al-Zamān still supposes, as he did in the night, that his father set the girl beside him. sirran, “secretly”, an adverbial accusative; its shadda and tanwīn are printed. li-ajli an, “for the sake of, so that”: li-, “for”, with ajl, “cause”, then an and the subjunctive. izdāda, Form VIII of zāda, “to increase”. فى is the edition's ى for final ي, though في stands beside it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ صَرَخَ عَلَى الْخَادِمِ الَّذِي هُوَ نَائِمٌ عَلَى الْبَابِ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ يَا مَلْعُونُ قُمْ عَلَى حَيْلِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu ṣarakha ʿalā al-khādimi alladhī huwa nāʾimun ʿalā al-bābi wa-qāla lahu waylaka yā malʿūnu qum ʿalā ḥaylika
sentences.l: Then indeed-he shouted at the-servant who he (is) sleeping at the-door, and-said to-him: Woe-to-you, O accursed-one, rise on your-strength!
sentences.i: Then he shouted for the servant who slept at the door, and said to him, “Curse you, you wretch, get up on your feet!”
sentences.n: thumma innahu, “then he”: innahu only marks a fresh start in the narrative. ṣarakha ʿalā, “to shout at, call out to”, is a usage of later Arabic. This is the servant set on guard at the door of the hall in the old tower where Qamar al-Zamān is shut up. waylaka, “woe to you”, an exclamation with the accusative. qum ʿalā ḥaylika, “stand up on your strength”, that is, “up on your feet”, as Budūr sat up ʿalā ḥaylihā two nights ago; ḥayl, “strength, power”.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْخَادِمُ وَهُوَ طَائِشُ الْعَقْلِ مِنَ النَّوْمِ وَقَدَّمَ الطَّشْتَ وَالْإِبْرِيقَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-khādimu wa-huwa ṭāʾishu al-ʿaqli mina al-nawmi wa-qaddama al-ṭashta wa-al-ibrīqa
sentences.l: And-rose the-servant while-he (was) giddy (of) the-mind from the-sleep, and-presented the-basin and-the-ewer.
sentences.i: The servant got up, his wits still scattered with sleep, and brought the basin and ewer.
sentences.n: ṭāʾish al-ʿaqli, “light of mind, giddy”: an adjective in construct with the thing it describes, a common Arabic turn; ṭāsha, “to be flighty, miss the mark”. Its ئ is printed. ṭasht and ibrīq, “basin and ewer”, are the vessels for washing before prayer; qaddama, Form II, “to set before”.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَدَخَلَ الْمُسْتَرَاحَ وَقَضَى حَاجَتَهُ وَخَرَجَ فَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى الصُّبْحَ وَجَلَسَ يُسَبِّحُ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-dakhala al-mustarāḥa wa-qaḍā ḥājatahu wa-kharaja fa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā al-ṣubḥa wa-jalasa yusabbiḥu Allāha taʿālā
sentences.l: And-rose Qamar al-Zamān, and-entered the-resting-place and-fulfilled his-need, and-came-out and-performed-ablution and-prayed the-morning (prayer), and-sat praising God (the) Exalted.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān got up, went into the privy and relieved himself, came out, made his ablutions, prayed the dawn prayer, and sat glorifying God the Exalted.
sentences.n: mustarāḥ, “place of rest”, is a polite name for the privy, and qaḍā ḥājatahu, “he fulfilled his need”, the usual phrase for relieving oneself. tawaḍḍaʾa, Form V, “to perform the ablution” before prayer. al-ṣubḥ, “the morning”, stands for the dawn prayer. sabbaḥa, Form II, “to glorify (God)”, by repeating subḥāna Allāh. The shadda and hamza of فتوضّأ and the shaddas of وصلّى and يسبّح are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إِلَى الْخَادِمِ فَوَجَدَهُ وَاقِفًا فِي خِدْمَتِهِ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara ilā al-khādimi fa-wajadahu wāqifan fī khidmatihi bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: Then he-looked at the-servant and-found-him standing in his-service between his-two-hands.
sentences.i: Then he looked at the servant and found him standing before him, ready to serve.
sentences.n: wāqifan, “standing”, the second object of wajada, “to find (someone) doing”. bayna yadayhi, “between his two hands”, that is, in front of him, the place of one in attendance.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ يَا صَوَابُ مَنْ جَاءَ هُنَا وَأَخَذَ الصَّبِيَّةَ مِنْ جَنْبِي وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu waylaka yā Ṣawābu man jāʾa hunā wa-akhadha al-ṣabiyyata min janbī wa-anā nāʾimun
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Woe-to-you, O Ṣawāb, who came here and-took the-girl from my-side while-I (was) sleeping?
sentences.i: And he said to him, “Curse you, Ṣawāb, who came in here and took the girl from my side while I was asleep?”
sentences.n: The servant is named here for the first time: Ṣawāb, “rightness”, a name of good omen of the kind given to slaves and eunuchs. jāʾa hunā, “came here”: hunā, “here”, is an adverb of place and needs no preposition. wa-anā nāʾimun, “while I was asleep”, a circumstantial clause with wa-. The shadda of الصبيّة is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَادِمُ يَاسَيِّدِي أَيُّ شَيْءٍ الصَّبِيَّةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khādimu yā sayyidī ayyu shayʾin al-ṣabiyyatu
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-servant: O my-master, what thing (is) the-girl?
sentences.i: The servant said to him, “My lord, what girl?”
sentences.n: The print runs يا and سيدي together as one word, ياسيدي, as it often does; the spacing is kept. ayyu shayʾin, “what thing?”, is the everyday “what?” of later Arabic, the source of colloquial ēsh: “what is this girl?”, that is, “what girl are you talking about?”. The shadda of الصبيّة is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الَّتِي كَانَتْ نَائِمَةً عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni al-ṣabiyyatu allatī kānat nāʾimatan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: And-said Qamar al-Zamān: The-girl who was sleeping with-me in this the-night.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said, “The girl who was sleeping beside me last night.”
sentences.n: fī hādhihi al-laylati, “in this night”, means the night just past. ʿindī, “with me, at my place”. The ئ of نائمة is printed.

sentences.t: فَانْزَعَجَ الْخَادِمُ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ مَاكَانَ عِنْدَكَ صَبِيَّةٌ وَلَاغَيْرُهَا وَمِنْ أَيْنَ دَخَلَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ عَلَى الْبَابِ وَهُوَ مَقْفُولٌ
sentences.tr: fa-inzaʿaja al-khādimu min kalāmihi wa-qāla lahu wa-Allāhi mā kāna ʿindaka ṣabiyyatun wa-lā ghayruhā wa-min ayna dakhalati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-anā nāʾimun ʿalā al-bābi wa-huwa maqfūlun
sentences.l: And-was-alarmed the-servant at his-words, and-said to-him: By-God, not was with-you a-girl and-not other-than-her; and-from where entered the-girl, while-I (was) sleeping at the-door and-it (was) locked?
sentences.i: The servant was alarmed at his words and said to him, “By God, there was no girl with you, nor anyone else. How could a girl have come in, when I was sleeping at the door, and it was locked?
sentences.n: inzaʿaja, Form VII, “to be disturbed, alarmed”; min gives the cause. The print runs ما and كان together, ماكان, and لا and غيرها, ولاغيرها; the spacing is kept in both. kāna stands in the masculine before its feminine subject ṣabiyyatun, which is allowed when words come between them. wa-lā ghayruhā, “nor other than her”, nor anyone at all. min ayna, “from where?”, here “how?”. maqfūl, “locked”, is the passive participle of qafala, “to lock”, a usage of later Arabic for Classical muqfal.

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدِي مَادَخَلَ عَلَيْكَ ذَكَرٌ وَلَا أُنْثَي
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi yā sayyidī mā dakhala ʿalayka dhakarun wa-lā unthā
sentences.l: By-God, O my-master, not entered upon-you a-male and-not a-female.
sentences.i: By God, my lord, no one came in to you, male or female.”
sentences.n: The print runs ما and دخل together as one word, مادخل; the spacing is kept. dakhala ʿalā, “to come in upon, enter the presence of”: ʿalā marks the one visited. dhakar wa-lā unthā, “male nor female”, a set pair meaning “nobody at all”. The print writes انثي with dotted ي for the final alif maqṣūra, a spelling habit the reverse of its usual ى for ي; it is read unthā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ تَكْذِبُ يَاعَبْدَ النَّحْسِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni takdhibu yā ʿabda al-naḥsi
sentences.l: And-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: You-lie, O slave (of) the-ill-omen!
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “You are lying, you ill-omened slave!
sentences.n: The print runs يا and عبد together, ياعبد; the spacing is kept. ʿabd al-naḥs, “slave of ill omen”: naḥs, “bad luck, ill omen”, is the word Budūr used of her father; here it is a common insult, “wretched slave”.

sentences.t: وَهَلْ وَصَلَ مِنْ قَدْرِكَ أَنْتَ الْآخَرُ أَنَّكَ تُخَادِعُنِي وَلَاتُخْبِرُنِى أَيْنَ ذَهَبَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الَّتِي كَانَتْ نَائِمَةً عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَلَمْ تُخْبِرْنِي بِالَّذِي أَخَذَهَا مِنْ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: wa-hal waṣala min qadrika anta al-ākharu annaka tukhādiʿunī wa-lā tukhbirunī ayna dhahabati al-ṣabiyyatu allatī kānat nāʾimatan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-lam tukhbirnī bi-alladhī akhadhahā min ʿindī
sentences.l: And-has it-reached, of your-worth, you the-other, that-you deceive-me and-do-not-tell-me where went the-girl who was sleeping with-me in this the-night, and-have-not told-me of-the-one-who took-her from with-me?
sentences.i: Has it come to this, that one as lowly as you, you of all people, should deceive me, and not tell me where the girl has gone who was sleeping beside me last night, nor tell me who it was that took her from me?”
sentences.n: The construction is loose and the exact sense is uncertain. waṣala min qadrika, “has it reached, of your worth”, seems to ask whether a creature of his low station has come so far as to deceive his master: “has it come to this, for one like you?”. anta al-ākharu, “you, the other”, is a turn of later Arabic, “you too, you for your part”, as Budūr said anā al-ukhrā in the last night; here it is scornful, “even you”. The آ of الآخر is printed. khādaʿa, Form III, “to deceive, trick”. The print runs لا and تخبرنى together as one word, ولاتخبرنى, with the edition's ى for final ي; the spacing is kept, though تخبرني follows with ي. akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to tell of”: bi- marks what is told, here alladhī, “the one who”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الطَّوَاشِي وَقَدِ انْزَعَجَ مِنْهُ وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدِي مَا رَأَيْتُ صَبِيَّةً وَلَا صَبِيًّا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ṭawāshī wa-qadi inzaʿaja minhu wa-Allāhi yā sayyidī mā raʾaytu ṣabiyyatan wa-lā ṣabiyyan
sentences.l: And-said the-eunuch, and he-had-become-alarmed at-him: By-God, O my-master, not I-saw a-girl and-not a-boy.
sentences.i: The eunuch, now thoroughly alarmed, said, “By God, my lord, I saw no girl and no boy.”
sentences.n: ṭawāshī, “eunuch”, a word of Turkish origin, is used of the servant interchangeably with khādim. wa-qadi inzaʿaja minhu, “when he had become alarmed at him”, a circumstantial clause with wa-qad and the perfect; qad takes a helping kasra before the joining alif. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَغَضِبَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ كَلَامِ الْخَادِمِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا مَلْعُونُ إِنَّ أَبِي عَلَّمَكَ الْمَكْرَ فَتَعَالَ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-ghaḍiba Qamaru al-Zamāni min kalāmi al-khādimi wa-qāla lahu yā malʿūnu inna abī ʿallamaka al-makra fa-taʿāla ʿindī
sentences.l: And-grew-angry Qamar al-Zamān at (the) words (of) the-servant, and-said to-him: O accursed-one, indeed my-father taught-you the-cunning; so-come to-me!
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān grew angry at the servant's words and said to him, “You accursed wretch, my father has taught you this trickery. Come here!”
sentences.n: ghaḍiba min, “to be angry at”: min gives the cause. makr, “cunning, trickery”. taʿāla, “come!”, an imperative used only in this form; ʿindī, “to me”, is the everyday preposition of later Arabic for Classical ilayya. The shadda of علّمك is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ الْخَادِمُ إِلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَمَسَكَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِأَطْوَاقِهِ وَضَرَبَ بِهِ الْأَرْضَ فَضَرَطَ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-khādimu ilā Qamari al-Zamāni fa-masaka Qamaru al-Zamāni bi-aṭwāqihi wa-ḍaraba bihi al-arḍa fa-ḍaraṭa
sentences.l: And-came-forward the-servant to Qamar al-Zamān, and-seized Qamar al-Zamān by-his-collars and-struck with-him the-ground, and-he-farted.
sentences.i: The servant came up to Qamar al-Zamān, and Qamar al-Zamān seized him by the collar and dashed him to the ground, and he farted.
sentences.n: The shadda of فتقدّم is printed. masaka bi-, “to seize, take hold of”: Classical prefers Form IV, amsaka bi-, and later Arabic uses the plain verb; bi- marks what is grasped. aṭwāq, plural of ṭawq, “collar, neck-ring”, here the neck of his garment; the plural is used loosely for the collar of one garment. ḍaraba bihi al-arḍa, “he struck the ground with him”, that is, he threw him down: bi- marks the thing struck with. ḍaraṭa, “to fart”: the fall knocks the wind out of the servant at both ends, a piece of the narrator's broad comedy.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَرَكَ عَلَيْهِ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَرَفَصَهُ بِرِجْلِهِ وَخَنَقَهُ حَتَّى غُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma baraka ʿalayhi Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-rafaṣahu bi-rijlihi wa-khanaqahu ḥattā ghushiya ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then knelt upon-him Qamar al-Zamān, and-kicked-him with-his-foot, and-throttled-him until it-was-swooned upon-him.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān knelt on him, kicked him and choked him until he fainted.
sentences.n: baraka ʿalā, “to kneel on”, properly said of a camel couching, here of pinning a man down with one's weight. رفصه is rafaṣahu, “he kicked him”, the later Arabic form with ṣād of Classical rafasa, “to kick”; it is read as printed. bi- marks the instrument, bi-rijlihi, “with his foot”. khanaqa, “to throttle”. ghushiya ʿalayhi, “there was a swooning upon him”, an impersonal passive: “he fainted”.

sentences.t: وَشَالَهُ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ وَرَبَطَهُ فِي سَلَبَةِ الْبِئْرِ وَأَدْلَاهُ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَ إِلَى الْمَاءِ وَأَرْخَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-shālahu baʿda dhālika wa-rabaṭahu fī salabati al-biʾri wa-adlāhu ilā an waṣala ilā al-māʾi wa-arkhāhu
sentences.l: And-lifted-him after that, and-tied-him to (the) rope (of) the-well, and-let-him-down until he-reached to the-water, and-let-him-go-slack.
sentences.i: After that he hoisted him up, tied him to the well rope and let him down until he reached the water, and let the rope run.
sentences.n: shāla, “to lift, carry”, is the everyday verb of later Arabic; Classical uses it of a camel raising its tail. rabaṭa fī, “to tie to”. salaba, “rope”, is a word of later, chiefly Egyptian, Arabic, especially for a rope of palm fibre; the vowels given here are those of current use and are not certain for the print. The ئ of البئر is printed. adlā, Form IV, “to let down (a bucket) into a well”: Qamar al-Zamān lowers the servant as one lowers a bucket. ilā an, “until”, with the perfect. arkhā, Form IV, “to slacken, let go”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الْأَيَّامُ أَيَّامَ بَرْدٍ وَشِتَاءٍ قَاطِعٍ فَغَطَسَ الْخَادِمُ فِى الْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tilka al-ayyāmu ayyāma bardin wa-shitāʾin qāṭiʿin fa-ghaṭasa al-khādimu fī al-māʾi
sentences.l: And-were those the-days days (of) cold and-winter cutting; and-sank the-servant in the-water.
sentences.i: Those were days of cold and bitter winter; and the servant went under in the water.
sentences.n: kānat … ayyāma, “those days were days of …”: the predicate of kāna is accusative. qāṭiʿ, “cutting, sharp”, of a winter that bites. ghaṭasa, “to plunge, go under”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَشَلَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَأَرْخَاهُ ثَانِيًا وَلَازَالَ يُغَطِّسُ ذٰلِكَ الْخَادِمَ فِى الْمَاءِ وَيَنْشُلُهُ مِنْهُ وَالْخَادِمُ يَسْتَغِيثُ وَيَصْرُخُ وَيَصِيحُ
sentences.tr: thumma nashalahu Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-arkhāhu thāniyan wa-lā zāla yughaṭṭisu dhālika al-khādima fī al-māʾi wa-yanshuluhu minhu wa-al-khādimu yastaghīthu wa-yaṣrukhu wa-yaṣīḥu
sentences.l: Then pulled-him-out Qamar al-Zamān and-let-him-down a-second-time; and-not-ceased dunking that the-servant in the-water and-pulling-him-out from-it, and-the-servant calling-for-help and-shrieking and-crying-out.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān hauled him out and let him down a second time, and he kept dunking the servant in the water and hauling him out again, while the servant called for help and shrieked and screamed.
sentences.n: nashala, “to snatch out, pull out”, as one takes meat from a pot. thāniyan, “a second time”, an adverbial accusative. The print runs لا and زال together as one word, ولازال; the spacing is kept. lā zāla, “did not cease”, with an imperfect, “kept on doing”: Classical Arabic says mā zāla of past time and keeps lā zāla for wishes, “may he not cease”, but later Arabic uses lā zāla freely for narrative. يغطس is read here as yughaṭṭisu, Form II, “to dunk”, since it takes an object; the unvowelled letters would also allow the plain verb, used transitively in later speech. istaghātha, Form X, “to call for help”. ṣarakha and ṣāḥa, “to shriek, cry out”, near synonyms piled up in the narrator's manner.

sentences.t: وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَقُولُ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ يَا مَلْعُونُ مَا أُطْلِعُكَ مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْبِئْرِ حَتَّى تُعْلِمَنِي وَتُخْبِرَنِي بِخَبَرِ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَقَضِيَّتِهَا وَمَنِ الَّذِي أَخَذَهَا وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni yaqūlu lahu wa-Allāhi yā malʿūnu mā uṭliʿuka min hādhihi al-biʾri ḥattā tuʿlimanī wa-tukhbiranī bi-khabari hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-qaḍiyyatihā wa-mani alladhī akhadhahā wa-anā nāʾimun
sentences.l: And-Qamar al-Zamān saying to-him: By-God, O accursed-one, not I-bring-you-up from this the-well until you-inform-me and-tell-me with-(the)-news (of) this the-girl and-her-affair, and-who (is) the-one-who took-her while-I (was) sleeping.
sentences.i: And Qamar al-Zamān was saying to him, “By God, you accursed wretch, I will not bring you up out of this well until you tell me and explain to me all about this girl and what has become of her, and who it was that took her while I slept.”
sentences.n: mā uṭliʿuka, “I will not bring you up”: mā with the imperfect for a future denial is the usage of later Arabic, where Classical would say lan uṭliʿaka. aṭlaʿa, Form IV, means in Classical Arabic “to let (someone) see, inform”; here it has the everyday sense “to bring up”, for which speech also uses Form II, ṭallaʿa. biʾr, “well”, is feminine, hence hādhihi. ḥattā with the subjunctive, “until”. akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. qaḍiyya, “affair, case”; its shadda is printed, as is that of الصبيّة and the ئ of البئر and نائم.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The name breaks across a line in the print, شهر | زاد, and is set here as the print's two parts.
